reason: The cited evidence shows oxidation occurs during wear (E1) and that oxide layers can form at 800 °C (E2), but none of the passages test or compare oxygen-rich versus inert atmospheres, measure the tribological effect of an in-situ formed oxide layer, or demonstrate that such a layer reduces friction and wear by acting as a lubricious barrier. The key premises about the protective role of the oxide layer and the effect of atmospheric control are unsupported by the provided evidence.
premises: Friction-induced oxidation occurs during wear of HEAs, producing surface oxides
An oxygen-rich atmosphere promotes formation of a continuous, adherent oxide tribolayer
This oxide layer acts as a lubricious and load-bearing barrier, reducing metal-to-metal contact
The oxide layer lowers friction and reduces wear compared to inert conditions where it does not form
The mechanism operates at elevated temperatures (600–800 °C) for alloys with oxide-forming elements
